## How to Use These Modules

These modules are for instructors who teach biomechanics, sport science or
control. Each one fits a single class session or a short problem set. Each
module gives:

- **Learning objectives** that say what a student should be able to do.
- **A reading path** through pages that already exist on this site.
- **Exercises** built on worked examples and interactive tools on this site.
- **Worked solutions**, folded so you can hand out the exercises first.

Every number in a solution comes from one of three places: a cited page, a
cited interactive tool, or a derivation shown in full on this page. Where an
exercise uses round numbers that are not on another page, the solution says so
and shows every step. These numbers are chosen to make the arithmetic easy to
follow. They are not measurements of golfers or clubs.

| Module | Suggested Course | Main Tool or Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [1. Orientation and Rotation Representations](#module-1) | Biomechanics, motion capture | [Rotation Representation Converter](../articles/rotation-converter.html) |
| [2. Constraint Torques at the Wrist](#module-2) | Biomechanics, multibody dynamics | [Cardan and Torque Projection Demonstration](../src/tools/wrist_universal_joint/grip_angle_simulator.html) |
| [3. Energy Accounting in the Proximal-Distal Chain](#module-3) | Sport science, mechanics | [Proximal-Distal Model Workbench](../articles/proximal-distal-model-workbench.html) |
| [4. Control-Affine Dynamics and Counterfactuals](#module-4) | Control, dynamical systems | Worked examples in the theory pages |

The modules can be taught in any order. Module 1 helps before Module 2, because
the wrist model uses rotation matrices.

## Module 1: Orientation and Rotation Representations {#module-1}

Motion-capture systems, simulators and papers describe the same orientation
in different ways. Students who can convert between them, and who know where
each one breaks, avoid a large class of analysis errors.

### Learning Objectives

- Convert one orientation between a rotation matrix, a unit quaternion, ZYX
  Euler angles, an axis-angle pair and a rotation vector.
- Explain why $q$ and $-q$ describe the same rotation.
- Show by hand why ZYX Euler angles lose one angle at a pitch of $90^\circ$,
  and say what the converter reports there.
- State what an orientation does not tell you, such as angular velocity or
  joint location.

### Reading Path

1. [Rotation Representation Converter](../articles/rotation-converter.html):
   read the Background and Mathematical Reference sections (about 20 minutes).
2. [Rotation Representations: A Cross-Reference Guide](../articles/rotation-representations-reference.html):
   the derivations behind each conversion (about 40 minutes).
3. [Rotations and SE(3)](../articles/The_Geometry_of_Motion/quarto/vol0_ch04_rotations_se3.html)
   in The Geometry of Motion, for a longer textbook treatment (optional).

### Exercises

All exercises use the converter's conventions: right-handed active rotations,
Hamilton quaternions ordered $(w,x,y,z)$, and intrinsic ZYX angles with
$R=R_z(\psi)R_y(\theta)R_x(\phi)$.

**Exercise 1.1 (Quarter Turn).** By hand, write the rotation matrix,
quaternion, axis-angle pair, rotation vector and ZYX angles for a $90^\circ$
rotation about $z$. Then press the **Rz(90°)** preset and check every panel.

**Exercise 1.2 (Two Quaternions, One Rotation).** Enter the quaternion
$(0,0,0,-1)$. Which quaternion does the converter report, and why is that not
a different rotation?

**Exercise 1.3 (The Arbitrary Preset).** The preset labelled
$\hat n=[1,1,1]/\sqrt3$, $47.3^\circ$ rotates about the diagonal axis.
Before pressing it, predict the trace of $R$, the quaternion and the rotation
vector. Then press the preset and compare.

**Exercise 1.4 (Gimbal Lock).** Enter yaw $\psi=30^\circ$, pitch
$\theta=90^\circ$ and roll $\phi=10^\circ$. Read the matrix panel. Then
enter $\psi=20^\circ$, $\theta=90^\circ$, $\phi=0^\circ$. Explain what you
see, and predict the Euler angles the converter reports if you press
**Use this R**.

### Worked Solutions

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 1.1"}
With $c=\cos 90^\circ=0$ and $s=\sin 90^\circ=1$,

$$
R_z(90^\circ)=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The quaternion for angle $\theta$ about unit axis $\hat n$ is
$(\cos\tfrac\theta2,\ \hat n\sin\tfrac\theta2)$. Here
$\cos 45^\circ=\sin 45^\circ=0.7071$, so $q=(0.7071,\,0,\,0,\,0.7071)$.
The axis-angle pair is $\hat n=(0,0,1)$, $\theta=90^\circ$. The rotation
vector is $\rho=\theta\hat n=(0,\,0,\,\pi/2)=(0,\,0,\,1.5708)$ rad. The ZYX
angles are $\psi=90^\circ$, $\theta=0$, $\phi=0$. The converter shows the same
values to more digits.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 1.2"}
The converter reports $(0,0,0,1)$. The quaternion-to-matrix formula on the
[converter page](../articles/rotation-converter.html) is quadratic in the
components, so $q$ and $-q$ give the same matrix. Both describe a $180^\circ$
turn about $z$. The converter picks the sign with $w\ge 0$ so that the reported
angle lies in $[0,\pi]$. At exactly $180^\circ$, $w=0$, so that rule cannot
decide; the converter's largest-component extraction returns $z=+1$. The axis
sign is a free choice here: $+z$ and $-z$ give the same half-turn. This is a reporting
convention, not a continuity rule. For a sampled swing you must choose signs
so that consecutive quaternions stay close.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 1.3"}
For any rotation, $\operatorname{tr}R=1+2\cos\theta$. With
$\theta=47.3^\circ$, $\cos\theta=0.6782$, so $\operatorname{tr}R=2.3563$.
The axis treats $x$, $y$ and $z$ alike, so the three diagonal entries are
equal: each is $2.3563/3=0.7854$. The converter's matrix is

$$
R=\begin{bmatrix}0.7854&-0.3170&0.5316\\0.5316&0.7854&-0.3170\\-0.3170&0.5316&0.7854\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The quaternion is $w=\cos 23.65^\circ=0.9160$ and each vector component is
$\sin 23.65^\circ/\sqrt3=0.2316$, so $q=(0.9160,\,0.2316,\,0.2316,\,0.2316)$.
The angle in radians is $47.3\pi/180=0.8255$, and each rotation-vector
component is $0.8255/\sqrt3=0.4766$ rad.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 1.4"}
Both entries give the same matrix. Its first row is
$(0,\,-0.3420,\,0.9397)=(0,\,-\sin 20^\circ,\,\cos 20^\circ)$. To see why,
multiply out the product at $\theta=90^\circ$:

$$
R_y(90^\circ)R_x(\phi)=\begin{bmatrix}0&\sin\phi&\cos\phi\\0&\cos\phi&-\sin\phi\\-1&0&0\end{bmatrix},
$$

$$
R_z(\psi)R_y(90^\circ)R_x(\phi)=\begin{bmatrix}0&-\sin(\psi-\phi)&\cos(\psi-\phi)\\0&\cos(\psi-\phi)&\sin(\psi-\phi)\\-1&0&0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Only the difference $\psi-\phi$ appears. Yaw $30^\circ$ with roll $10^\circ$
and yaw $20^\circ$ with roll $0^\circ$ both give $\psi-\phi=20^\circ$. When
the matrix is the input, the converter detects the lock and sets roll to zero,
so it reports $\psi=20^\circ$, $\theta=90^\circ$, $\phi=0^\circ$ with a
gimbal-lock warning. The body can still rotate in every direction. Only this
choice of three angles has stopped describing it uniquely.
:::

## Module 2: Constraint Torques at the Wrist {#module-2}

A two-axis wrist model can carry a torque along a direction in which it does
not allow rotation. This module separates that constraint torque from
actuation, energy and grip claims.

### Learning Objectives

- Find the direction of an ideal universal joint's reaction couple and check
  that it does no work on the allowed motion.
- Show with a small example that a constraint reaction can change when the
  actuator input changes.
- Compute a club's transverse inertia about the grip from point-mass and
  thin-rod terms.
- Use the Cardan demonstration to tell a supported driveshaft apart from a
  wrist, and explain why a torque ratio above one is not an efficiency above
  one.
- Derive how a constant torque error grows into an angle error.

### Reading Path

1. [Constraint Torques at the Wrist](../articles/wrist-universal-joint.html):
   read through "The Grip Angle Hypothesis" and "The Cardan Driveshaft
   Analogy" (about 60 minutes).
2. [The Null Space of the Constraint Jacobian](../articles/null-space-constraint-jacobian.html):
   the motion a constraint still allows (about 30 minutes).
3. [Screw Theory Reference](../articles/screw-theory-reference.html):
   wrenches, twists and reciprocity (optional).
4. [Cardan and Torque Projection Demonstration](../src/tools/wrist_universal_joint/grip_angle_simulator.html):
   the interactive tool used in Exercises 2.3 and 2.4.

### Exercises

**Exercise 2.1 (Reaction Direction).** Model the wrist as
$R=R_x(\phi)R_y(\psi)$ with allowed rotation directions
$\mathbf a=\mathbf e_x$ and $\mathbf b=R_x(\phi)\mathbf e_y$ in the forearm
frame. At $\phi=30^\circ$, $\psi=20^\circ$, find the unit reaction direction
$\mathbf n_c$ in the forearm frame and in the hand frame. Check that it does
no work on the allowed motion.

**Exercise 2.2 (A Reaction That Depends on the Input).** Take
$M=\begin{bmatrix}2&0&0.5\\0&2&0\\0.5&0&2\end{bmatrix}$, the constraint
$A=(0,0,1)$, inputs $B=(\mathbf e_x,\mathbf e_y)$ and no bias. Apply the
input $(u,0)$. Find $\ddot q_x$ and the multiplier $\lambda$ two ways: by
substitution, and with the wrist page's formula
$\partial\lambda/\partial u=-(AM^{-1}A^T)^{-1}AM^{-1}B$.

**Exercise 2.3 (The Cardan Demonstration).** Open the demonstration and set
Demo Angle to $30^\circ$. Read the Angular Velocity Ratio and Torque
Transmission Ratio in Model Information at Input Shaft Phase $0^\circ$ and
$60^\circ$. Derive both readings, and explain why a torque ratio above one
does not mean the joint creates energy.

**Exercise 2.4 (Grip-Point Inertia).** With the demonstration's default club
properties (200 g head at 0.85 m, 100 g shaft of length 1.00 m), the tool
reports $I_\alpha$. Derive it. Then explain why the tool's
$I_\gamma=0.5\,I_\alpha$ is not a measured club property.

**Exercise 2.5 (How a Torque Error Grows).** A constant torque error $\eta$
with standard deviation $\sigma_\tau$ acts on a single inertia $I$ for time
$T$, starting from zero angle and velocity error. Derive the angle standard
deviation $\sigma_\theta$. Evaluate it for $\sigma_\tau=0.15$ N m,
$T=0.010$ s and $I=0.005$ or $0.00015$ kg m², the illustrative values on the
wrist page.

### Worked Solutions

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 2.1"}
The ideal reaction couple must do no work on any allowed rotation, so it is
perpendicular to both $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$:
$\mathbf n_c=\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=R_x(\phi)\mathbf e_z=(0,\,-\sin\phi,\,\cos\phi)$.
At $\phi=30^\circ$ this is $(0,\,-0.500000,\,0.866025)$ in the forearm frame.

In the hand frame,
${}^H\mathbf n_c=R^T\mathbf n_c=R_y(\psi)^TR_x(\phi)^TR_x(\phi)\mathbf e_z=R_y(\psi)^T\mathbf e_z=(-\sin\psi,\,0,\,\cos\psi)$.
At $\psi=20^\circ$ this is $(-0.342020,\,0,\,0.939693)$. Both match the
[wrist page](../articles/wrist-universal-joint.html).

Check: $\mathbf n_c\cdot\mathbf a=0$ because the first component is zero, and
$\mathbf n_c\cdot\mathbf b=-\sin\phi\cos\phi+\cos\phi\sin\phi=0$, with
$\mathbf b=(0,\cos\phi,\sin\phi)$. So the couple does no work on any allowed
relative rotation $\mathbf a\dot\phi+\mathbf b\dot\psi$. The direction moves
with the wrist: it is neither a fixed forearm axis nor a fixed hand axis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 2.2"}
**By substitution.** The constraint forces $\ddot q_z=0$. The equations
$M\ddot q=Bu+A^T\lambda$ read

$$
2\ddot q_x+0.5\ddot q_z=u,\qquad 2\ddot q_y=0,\qquad 0.5\ddot q_x+2\ddot q_z=\lambda.
$$

With $\ddot q_z=0$, the first gives $\ddot q_x=u/2$, and the third gives
$\lambda=0.5\cdot u/2$, so $\lambda=u/4$.

**By the formula.** The $x$–$z$ block of $M$ has determinant
$2\cdot2-0.5^2=3.75$, so $AM^{-1}A^T=2/3.75=0.5333$ and the $x$ entry of
$AM^{-1}B$ is $-0.5/3.75=-0.1333$. The $y$ entry is zero. Then
$\partial\lambda/\partial u=-(-0.1333)/0.5333=0.25$, which again gives
$\lambda=u/4$.

A changed input changes the reaction at the same state. This disproves the
claim that every constraint load is drift that the input cannot affect. It
does not show that any desired reaction can be chosen freely.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 2.3"}
The [wrist page](../articles/wrist-universal-joint.html) gives the
supported-shaft speed ratio
$\dot\chi/\dot\varphi=\cos\delta/(1-\sin^2\delta\sin^2\varphi)$, and the
demonstration computes exactly this. With $\delta=30^\circ$,
$\cos\delta=0.866025$ and $\sin^2\delta=0.25$.

- At phase $0^\circ$, $\sin\varphi=0$, so the speed ratio is $0.8660$ and the
  torque ratio, its reciprocal, is $1.1547$.
- At phase $60^\circ$, $\sin^2\varphi=0.75$, so the denominator is
  $1-0.25\cdot0.75=0.8125$. The speed ratio is $0.866025/0.8125=1.0659$
  and the torque ratio is $0.9382$.

For a lossless joint with fixed supports, input power equals output power:
$\tau_{\rm in}\dot\varphi=\tau_{\rm out}\dot\chi$. Torque goes up exactly
when speed goes down, so the product of the two ratios is one. This is a
driveshaft held in two bearings. It is not the freely moving wrist, and the
demonstration's phase is not a wrist angle.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 2.4"}
About the grip, a point head contributes $mr^2$ and a thin uniform shaft
contributes $\tfrac13mL^2$:

$$
I_\alpha=0.200(0.85)^2+\tfrac13(0.100)(1.00)^2=0.1445+0.0333=0.177833\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2},
$$

which the tool shows as $0.1778$ kg m². This matches the
[wrist page](../articles/wrist-universal-joint.html). The tool then sets
$I_\gamma=0.5\,I_\alpha$, and its source labels this an illustrative ratio. A
real shaft-axis inertia needs the shaft radius, the head's own inertia and its
offset from the shaft. As the wrist page says, an assumed ratio does not
become a measured property by appearing in a simulator.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 2.5"}
With constant $\eta$, the angular acceleration is $\eta/I$. Integrating twice
from zero gives $\delta\omega(T)=T\eta/I$ and $\delta\theta(T)=T^2\eta/(2I)$.
The standard deviation scales the same way:
$\sigma_\theta=T^2\sigma_\tau/(2I)$.

- With $I=0.005$: $\sigma_\theta=(0.010)^2(0.15)/(2\cdot0.005)=0.0015$ rad.
- With $I=0.00015$: $\sigma_\theta=(0.010)^2(0.15)/(2\cdot0.00015)=0.0500$ rad.

The ratio is $0.005/0.00015=33.333$, as in the table on the
[wrist page](../articles/wrist-universal-joint.html). Both inertias are
illustrative and unmeasured. The result shows how sensitivity scales with
inertia under these assumptions. It is not a clubface error or a grip
comparison.
:::

## Module 3: Energy Accounting in the Proximal-Distal Chain {#module-3}

Coaches and textbooks often say energy "flows" from the body to the club.
This module teaches students to check that kind of claim with a clear system
boundary, a consistent model and a stated falsifier.

### Learning Objectives

- Show how two mass models of the same club give different kinetic energies
  for the same motion.
- Compute the net force and moment from two hand forces, and recognize a pure
  couple.
- Tell an instantaneous counterfactual apart from a forward one, and say what
  result would count against a stated mechanism.

### Reading Path

1. [How a Golf Swing Carries Energy](../articles/proximal-distal-a-journey-through-the-swing.html):
   the visual narrative (about 30 minutes).
2. [Explore the Proximal–Distal Models](../articles/proximal-distal-model-workbench.html):
   read "What Would Count Against the Mechanism?" and "Read Work and Energy
   With the Same Model" (about 40 minutes). Students who install the
   workbench can run the guided experiments it lists.
3. [Proximal-to-Distal Energy Transfer](../articles/proximal-distal-energy-transfer.html):
   the technical summary (optional).

### Exercises

**Exercise 3.1 (Two Models of One Club).** One part of the workbench puts the
shaft mass $m_2$ at the club tip with the head mass $m_c$. Another part treats
the shaft as a uniform rod. With the arm still and the club turning at
$\omega$, write the club's kinetic energy in each model. Evaluate both for
$m_2=3$ kg, $m_c=1$ kg, $L_2=1$ m and $\omega=2$ rad/s, the test values on
the workbench page.

**Exercise 3.2 (Two Hands, One Couple).** The hands are 0.1 m apart along the
shaft, so $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_R-\mathbf r_L=(0,0,0.1)$ m. The right hand
pushes on the club with $\mathbf f_R=(10,0,0)$ N and the left hand with
$\mathbf f_L=(-10,0,0)$ N. There are no contact moments. Find the net force
and the moment about the midpoint. Does the moment change if you take it
about the right hand instead? These round numbers are chosen for this exercise
only.

**Exercise 3.3 (What Would Count Against It?).** A student turns off the wrist
torque at one instant, sees no change in the club's acceleration at that
instant, and concludes that the wrist does nothing. Using the workbench page,
explain what is wrong with this test and describe a better one.

### Worked Solutions

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 3.1"}
With the arm still, the club spins about the grip. A point mass at distance
$L_2$ has speed $L_2\omega$, and a uniform rod has inertia $\tfrac13m_2L_2^2$
about its end. So

$$
T_{\mathrm{tip}}=\tfrac12(m_2+m_c)L_2^2\omega^2,\qquad
T_{\mathrm{rod}}=\tfrac12(m_2/3+m_c)L_2^2\omega^2.
$$

With the given values, $T_{\mathrm{tip}}=\tfrac12(4)(1)(4)=8$ J and
$T_{\mathrm{rod}}=\tfrac12(2)(1)(4)=4$ J. The two parts of the same tool
disagree by a factor of two on the same state, as the
[workbench page](../articles/proximal-distal-model-workbench.html) warns. Any
energy-transfer comparison must fix this mismatch first.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 3.2"}
The net force is $\mathbf F=\mathbf f_R+\mathbf f_L=(0,0,0)$. The moment
about the midpoint, from the
[workbench page](../articles/proximal-distal-model-workbench.html), is

$$
\mathbf M_{\mathrm{mid}}=\frac{\mathbf d}{2}\times(\mathbf f_R-\mathbf f_L)
=(0,0,0.05)\times(20,0,0)=(0,1,0)\ \mathrm{N\,m}.
$$

The cross product uses
$(a\times b)_y=a_zb_x-a_xb_z=0.05\cdot20-0=1$; the other two components are
zero. Because the net force is zero, this is a pure couple, and its moment is
the same about every point. About the right hand, only the left force has a
moment arm: $(\mathbf r_L-\mathbf r_R)\times\mathbf f_L=(0,0,-0.1)\times(-10,0,0)=(0,1,0)$
N m. The hands turn the club without pushing it anywhere.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 3.3"}
The [workbench page](../articles/proximal-distal-model-workbench.html) gives
three reasons. First, an instantaneous change only measures
$G(x)(u_1-u_0)$ at one state. Symmetry, cancellation or the choice of output
can make that change zero even when the torque matters later. Second, the
later effect of removing the torque includes the changed state, so it needs a
forward counterfactual that starts from the same cut state and runs on.
Third, the test did not say in advance what result it expected.

A better test states, before running it, the observable (for example club
speed at a defined event), the time window, what stays the same (stored
elastic energy, damping, contact) and the size of effect expected. It then
runs the matched forward counterfactual, a negative control and a step-size
check. A failure of that stated, nonzero prediction would count against the
mechanism.
:::

## Module 4: Control-Affine Dynamics and Counterfactuals {#module-4}

The theory pages on this site each include a worked example whose numbers
come from code in the repository. This module turns four of them into a
problem set for a control or dynamical-systems course.

### Learning Objectives

- Evaluate the drift of a pendulum and linearize it at a state.
- Show that the width of a reachable set does not depend on a constant drift,
  even when the Drift-Control Ratio (DCR) is large.
- Explain why the response of a control-affine system is affine in its input,
  and check the superposition identity with numbers.
- Distinguish a single pointwise drift sample from a forward zero-torque
  trajectory.

### Reading Path

1. [Part 4: Worked Pendulum Dynamics](../articles/theory-part4.html)
   (about 40 minutes).
2. [Drift, Control Capacity and Golf-Swing Correction](../articles/drift-control-ratio.html):
   read the worked example on reachable width (about 30 minutes).
3. [Superposition in Affine Control Systems](../articles/superposition.html): read the worked example on
   the double pendulum (about 30 minutes).
4. [Zero-Torque Counterfactual (ZTCF) Family](../articles/zero-torque-counterfactual.html):
   read the worked example on a pointwise sample (about 30 minutes).

### Exercises

**Exercise 4.1 (Pendulum Drift and Linearization).** For a rigid pendulum
$\dot x=(\dot\theta,\ -g\sin\theta/L+u/(mL^2))$ with $m=1$ kg, $L=1$ m,
$g=9.81$ m/s², evaluate the drift at $\theta=0.5$ rad, $\dot\theta=0$, $u=0$,
and find the linearization $A$ at that state.

**Exercise 4.2 (Reachable Width).** For $\dot x=d+u$ with $x(0)=0$,
$|u(t)|\le1$ and horizon $T=1$, find the set of reachable $x(1)$ for $d=0$ and
for $d=100$. What does this say about using the size of $d$ relative to $u$
as a measure of control?

**Exercise 4.3 (Superposition).** The superposition page defines
$\Phi(\tau)=M(q)^{-1}(\tau-C(q,\dot q)\dot q)$ for a double pendulum and
reports $\Phi(0)$, $\Phi(\tau_1)$ and $\Phi(\tau_2)$ for $\tau_1=(2,0)$ and
$\tau_2=(0,1)$ N m. Use only those three results to predict
$\Phi(\tau_1+\tau_2)$, then compare with the page. Why can this identity never
fail?

**Exercise 4.4 (One Drift Sample).** Reproduce the zero-torque page's
pointwise sample for the default three-link model at rest, using the code
below. Explain why this sample alone does not predict the club's path with
the torques removed.

```python
import numpy as np
from src.affine_control.golf_model import GolfModel

GolfModel().drift_acceleration(np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3))
```

### Worked Solutions

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 4.1"}
With $\sin 0.5=0.479426$ and $\cos 0.5=0.877583$, the drift is
$\dot x=(0,\ -9.81\cdot0.479426)=(0,\ -4.7032)$, in rad/s and rad/s². The
Jacobian of $-g\sin\theta/L$ with respect to $\theta$ is $-g\cos\theta/L$, so

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-9.81\cdot0.877583&0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-8.6091&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

These match the worked example on
[Part 4](../articles/theory-part4.html), which computes them with
`SimplePendulum` in `src/tangent_models/examples.py`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 4.2"}
Integrate: $x(1)=d\cdot1+\int_0^1u\,dt$. The integral can take any value
from $-1$ to $1$. So the reachable set is $[-1,1]$ for $d=0$ and
$[99,101]$ for $d=100$. Both have width 2. A large drift moves the set but does
not shrink it, so the control still has the same authority. A ratio of drift
size to control size rose from 0 to 100 without any change in what the control
can do. This matches the worked example on the
[Drift-Control Ratio page](../articles/drift-control-ratio.html).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 4.3"}
From the [superposition page](../articles/superposition.html),
$\Phi(0)=(-0.7709,\,2.5089)$, $\Phi(\tau_1)=(1.8448,\,-1.1359)$ and
$\Phi(\tau_2)=(-2.5933,\,9.0483)$. Then

$$
\Phi(\tau_1)+\Phi(\tau_2)-\Phi(0)=(1.8448-2.5933+0.7709,\ -1.1359+9.0483-2.5089)=(0.0224,\ 5.4035),
$$

which is the page's value for $\Phi(\tau_1+\tau_2)$. The identity cannot fail
because $\Phi(\tau)=M^{-1}\tau-M^{-1}C\dot q$ is a fixed matrix times $\tau$
plus a fixed vector, at a fixed state. Subtracting $\Phi(0)$ removes the
fixed vector once, which is why it appears with a minus sign. The numbers
illustrate the theorem; they do not test it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution to Exercise 4.4"}
The call returns about $(-31.40,\ 29.98,\ 1.57)$ rad/s², the value on the
[zero-torque page](../articles/zero-torque-counterfactual.html). At rest the
velocity terms are zero, so this is the acceleration that gravity alone would
cause at that one state. It is a single sample of the drift $f(x)$. The
forward zero-torque trajectory starts from a state and then evolves under the
drift alone, so the state, and the drift, change at every later instant.
Predicting that path requires integrating the equations forward; one sample
cannot do it.
:::
